Firstling
FURST-ling
noun
From first with the diminutive suffix -ling, denoting the young of a creature; hence the firstborn of a beast — the first male to open the matrix of herd or flock.

Biblical Definition

A firstling is the firstborn male of a beast, the first to open the matrix of herd or flock, and by the LORD’s claim it was never the owner’s to keep. The word enters Scripture at the first act of worship recorded after Eden: “And Abel, he also brought of the firstlings of his flock and of the fat thereof. And the LORD had respect unto Abel and to his offering” (Gen 4:4). The difference between the brothers was not agriculture but faith and blood — “By faith Abel offered unto God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain” (Heb 11:4) — and Abel gave the firstborn and the fat, the best and the first, not the leavings. Under the law the claim was formalized: every firstling male of herd and flock was to be sanctified to the LORD, put to no work, unshorn (Deu 15:19), and if clean, its blood sprinkled on the altar and its fat burned, for “they are holy” (Num 18:17). But the ass was unclean and could not be offered, and here the law preaches the gospel with terrible plainness: “every firstling of an ass thou shalt redeem with a lamb; and if thou wilt not redeem it, then thou shalt break his neck” (Exo 13:13). A lamb dies in its place, or it dies itself. There is no third way for the unclean firstling, and none for us.

Webster 1828 Definition

The first produce or offspring of a beast; the firstborn of herd or flock, claimed by the LORD.

expand to see more

FIRSTLING, the first produce or offspring; applied to beasts, as the firstling of a cow, a sheep, an ass.

From first and the diminutive -ling; the male that first openeth the matrix.

Abel brought of the firstlings of his flock and of the fat thereof (Gen 4:4).

Clean firstlings were sacrificed and not redeemed; they are holy (Num 18:17).

The firstling of an ass, being unclean, was redeemed with a lamb or its neck broken (Exo 13:13).

Key Scripture

Gen 4:4 — "And Abel, he also brought of the firstlings of his flock and of the fat thereof. And the LORD had respect unto Abel and to his offering:"

Heb 11:4 — "By faith Abel offered unto God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain, by which he obtained witness that he was righteous, God testifying of his gifts: and by it he being dead yet speaketh."

Exo 13:13 — "And every firstling of an ass thou shalt redeem with a lamb; and if thou wilt not redeem it, then thou shalt break his neck: and all the firstborn of man among thy children shalt thou redeem."

Num 18:17 — "But the firstling of a cow, or the firstling of a sheep, or the firstling of a goat, thou shalt not redeem; they are holy: thou shalt sprinkle their blood upon the altar, and shalt burn their fat for an offering made by fire, for a sweet savour unto the LORD."

Modern Corruption

Abel’s firstlings are read as a lesson in generosity or in agrarian sentiment, when the text is about faith and substitutionary blood — and the ass’s broken neck refuses every soft gospel.

expand to see more

The first corruption is moralizing. Abel’s offering is preached as a lesson in giving God your best, and Cain’s as the stinginess of a man who kept back the good fruit — a stewardship sermon lifted out of a passage about atonement. Give it its weight. Abel brought a slain firstling and its fat; Cain brought the produce of ground that God had cursed, bloodlessly, on his own terms. Hebrews does not say Abel’s sacrifice was larger, but that it was offered by faith, and that by it he obtained witness that he was righteous. The difference was not quantity of devotion but the ground of acceptance: a life laid down in the sinner’s room, received by faith, versus a worship of man’s own devising. The second corruption is the sentimental reading of the firstling of the ass — the modern instinct that recoils from the broken neck and quietly drops the verse. But the verse is the whole gospel in one sentence, and softening it costs everything.

Set the two firstlings side by side. The clean firstling was holy and could not be redeemed: its blood went to the altar, for it was the offering itself — and that is Christ, the firstborn of every creature, whose blood was never to be exchanged for another. The unclean firstling — the ass, the beast of burden, useful and dirty, exactly the sinner’s emblem — had no worth to bring to God at all. For it the law appointed one alternative and no more: a lamb dies in its stead, or its own neck is broken (Exo 13:13; Exo 34:20). No third option is offered, no improvement of the ass, no delay, no partial payment. Either substitution or death. Every Israelite child who watched a lamb led out for the family donkey was being catechized in the doctrine of particular redemption before he could read, and the same terms stand at the Judgment: Christ in your room, or your own soul answering for itself for ever.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The firstborn male of a beast, claimed by the LORD; the emblem of both the Lamb offered and the sinner redeemed.

expand to see more

Firstling — first + -ling; the firstborn of herd or flock.

Hebrew bekor / peter, the male that first openeth the matrix.

Abel’s firstlings and their fat were accepted; Cain’s bloodless offering was not (Gen 4:4).

Clean firstlings were not redeemed but sacrificed — they are holy (Num 18:17).

The firstling of an ass: redeemed with a lamb, or its neck broken (Exo 13:13).

Usage

"Abel brought the firstlings and the fat — the best and the first, and by faith."

"A clean firstling could not be redeemed; it was the offering."

"Redeemed with a lamb or its neck broken: the unclean firstling has no third option."
